questions.question: Explain why the Sun is classified as a star. Give its approximate diameter compared with Earth, its main components and the temperatures of its surface and core.
questions.expected_answer: A star is a huge luminous ball of hot gas (plasma) held together by gravity that produces its own energy by nuclear reactions in its core; the Sun does this, so it is a star (the nearest one). Diameter about 1.4 million km, about 109 times Earth's. Mainly hydrogen (about three quarters) and helium (about a quarter) with small amounts of heavier elements. Surface (photosphere) about 5 500 °C; core about 15 million °C.

questions.question: Describe nuclear fusion in the Sun's core: the reactants and product, why extreme conditions are needed, and where the energy comes from. Why is the Sun not 'on fire'?
questions.expected_answer: In the core, hydrogen nuclei (protons) are fused in steps into helium nuclei: four hydrogen nuclei make one helium nucleus. Hydrogen nuclei are positively charged and repel each other, so very high temperature (about 15 million °C, giving fast nuclei) and very high pressure/density (from the weight of the outer layers, giving frequent collisions) are needed to bring them close enough to fuse. The helium nucleus has slightly less mass than the four hydrogen nuclei; the missing mass is converted to energy (E = mc²). The Sun is not on fire: burning is a chemical reaction with oxygen that rearranges atoms, while fusion changes nuclei and releases millions of times more energy per kilogram.

questions.question: Explain how energy from the Sun's core reaches Earth and why this energy is essential for life. Give one danger of the Sun's radiation.
questions.expected_answer: Energy from fusion moves outward slowly through the dense inner Sun by radiation (absorbed and re-emitted many times, taking tens of thousands of years or more), then by convection in the outer layers, and is radiated from the surface as light, infrared and ultraviolet radiation. It crosses the vacuum of space at the speed of light, reaching Earth in about 8 min 20 s. Plants use sunlight for photosynthesis, the start of almost all food chains; it warms the Earth and drives winds, ocean currents and the water cycle; fossil fuels store ancient solar energy. Danger: ultraviolet radiation causes sunburn, eye damage and skin cancer.
